title: Dispute resolution: Assistance differs from machine adjudication
desc: Frames AAA experimentation around process redesign and legitimacy, with efficiency and reliability claims exceeding supplied evidence.

kps.k: The central proposition is that AI could expand dispute resolution, not merely make existing legal work cheaper.
kps.d: Bridget McCormack argues that simpler, lower-cost processes could serve individuals and resource-constrained organisations that currently abandon valid civil claims. She illustrates the gap with personal-injury claims that cannot attract lawyers yet remain too procedurally demanding for self-representation. Her endorsement concerns relief for non-frivolous claims, not litigation growth indiscriminately. Her claim that 92% of Americans cannot afford civil legal help lacks an underlying study in the supplied material; the interviews offer no measured improvement in access or outcomes.

qs.q: But we think with this technology, we can build and offer dispute resolution services, options, new products, so that any party that wants to resolve a dispute will have an option they can afford and that will suit them.
qs.a: An AI Arbitrator? The Latest Innovations from the American Arbitration Association, with CEO Bridget McCormack and CTO Diana Didia · Regulators & courts · 2025

qs.q: Bridget McCormack: I do think the ability for more people with non-frivolous lawsuits to get relief for those wrongs is a good thing.
qs.a: Generative AI and the Courts: Expanding Legal Access or Opening the Floodgates? — full episode transcript · Regulators & courts · 2025

kps.k: The main divide concerns whether AI should assist adjudicators or replace them.
kps.d: AAA’s planned November 2025 AI arbitrator starts with documents-only construction disputes: AI drafts awards, while a human arbitrator verifies and approves the final decision. McCormack retains party choice and human-led processes, particularly where relationships matter; removing humans remains a conditional future possibility. By contrast, Fortuna Arbitration’s founders present Arbitrus as end-to-end automated adjudication that replaces human arbitrators. Bob Ambrogi explicitly leaves open whether some aspects of legal decision-making require human judgment. These are contrasting deployment propositions, not comparative performance findings.

qs.q: This is an AI system that will actually draft arbitration awards with a human arbitrator validating and signing off on the final decision before it goes out.
qs.a: An AI Arbitrator? The Latest Innovations from the American Arbitration Association, with CEO Bridget McCormack and CTO Diana Didia · Regulators & courts · 2025

qs.q: And this first use case is just documents-only construction cases.

kps.k: AAA treats AI adoption as redesigning the dispute-resolution process around domain expertise and user needs.
kps.d: AAA reports combining internal development, acquired teams and partners. Clause Builder AI converts its clause library and review experience into natural-language drafting assistance, without demonstrated accuracy or guaranteed enforceability. Its adjudication strategy uses prior awards and expertise to train agents, starting with a documentary task that excludes testimony. McCormack distinguishes a planned organisation-wide case-management replacement by the end of 2027 from adjudication tools that expand case type by case type only where relevant data and expertise exist. The practical principle is to match the process to the dispute, rather than automate every matter identically.

qs.q: So, we trained a GPT-based large language model on that internal data and created a natural language interface.

qs.q: We have all this expertise and all these awards that we were able to turn into the handbook to train the agents that are working across the arbitration process.

kps.k: Efficiency and reliability claims substantially exceed the performance evidence supplied.
kps.d: AAA predicts lower costs and shorter resolution times but supplies implementation accounts rather than measured results. Arbitrus promises arbitration costs falling from an asserted $100,000 average to $10,000 and decisions within 72 hours. Ambrogi reports company testing with zero hallucinations across 100 cases, but the excerpts provide neither methodology nor independent validation. The founders attribute reliability to a hybrid of LLMs and separate machine-learning models for factual and honesty-related judgments. Their reported hallucination result does not establish the broader claims of unbiased, accurate or consistently sound adjudication.

qs.q: It's going to significantly reduce cost and time to resolution, and we're pretty excited for the world to see it.
qs.a: Live from MAICON 2025: Building AAA's First AI Arbitrator — full episode transcript · Regulators & courts · 2025

qs.q: The system promises to cut the cost of arbitration from an average of $100,000 to just $10,000 while delivering consistent, unbiased decisions within 72 hours.
qs.a: Ep 280: Is Arbitrus.ai the Future of Dispute Resolution? · Legal-tech vendor · 2025

kps.k: The legitimacy debate turns on procedural confidence, human fallibility and the distinction between assistance and decision-making.
kps.d: McCormack expects explanations and explicit acknowledgment of claims to help parties feel heard. She invokes mainly litigation-based procedural-justice literature and personal experience, not results from AAA’s AI arbitration. Zach Abramowitz challenges resistance to adjudicator AI by citing human error and a reported survey showing nearly 90% support for lawyers’ research and analytics use versus 23% for judges or arbitrators making decisions. His description of a double standard compares different tasks. Courtroom hallucination incidents and judges’ reported deepfake concerns supply countervailing reasons for caution, but do not quantify system-wide error or prove that either human or AI adjudication performs better.

qs.q: And then when they get an award, it will explain, "Here's why the answer is A and not B." I really think that ability to give people some assurance that they were understood is a game changer.
qs.a: Live from MAICON 2025: Building AAA's First AI Arbitrator — full episode transcript · Regulators & courts · 2025

qs.q: And that literature shows that parties that feel like a court, it's mostly done around litigation, that a court understood their complaints and allowed them to say why they felt like they were wronged or not wronged, from your perspective.
qs.a: An AI Arbitrator? The Latest Innovations from the American Arbitration Association, with CEO Bridget McCormack and CTO Diana Didia · Regulators & courts · 2025

kps.k: Concrete safeguards favour bounded, reviewed uses, while governance and validation remain unfinished.
kps.d: Leonard’s account of Pennsylvania’s interim judicial policy permits defined low-risk tasks using approved tools, human review, confidentiality protections and leadership oversight; it does not authorise autonomous adjudication. AAA describes arbitrator participation, first-time-user testing and continuing iteration, and promises an independent academic white paper whose findings are not supplied. Diana Didia also identifies model-release governance as unresolved. These accounts distinguish permission and development safeguards from demonstrated safety or effectiveness.

qs.q: So the Pennsylvania Supreme Court (which is the jurisdiction where I'm licensed) now allows the use of approved generative AI tools for certain defined, low-risk tasks, as long as there is human review, strict confidentiality, and leadership oversight.
qs.a: Can Judges Use AI? Inside the Pennsylvania Supreme Court's Interim Policy — full episode transcript · Regulators & courts · 2025

qs.q: We wanted them to use it as first-time users who know nothing about arbitration: How does it work for you?

kps.k: Providers envisage both more resolved disputes and earlier settlement or prevention, with different implications for professional work.
kps.d: McCormack predicts that simpler processes could multiply AAA’s roughly half-million annual disputes tenfold and sustain arbitrators who adapt their business models. Didia proposes reusing agents for early case evaluation and settlement. Arbitrus’s founders instead emphasise predictable contractual outcomes that help general counsel anticipate success and prevent disputes, alongside a longer-term private legal-system ambition. These remain forecasts and proposed uses, not demonstrated demand, settlement gains or employment outcomes. Enterprise efficiency benefits are distinct from the access-to-justice objective of serving unmet civil legal need.

qs.q: uh know, making the process just simpler for users is gonna mean that if right now we resolve half the million disputes a year, we can resolve 10x that.

kps.k: Implementation requires organisational change and professional learning, but enthusiasm should not be mistaken for outcome evidence.
kps.d: McCormack treats AAA’s longstanding expertise as both an asset and a barrier to changing successful legacy practices. She recommends deliberate change management with acquisitions as only part of the solution; AAA reports recruiting people who combine legal and technical skills. Leonard frames the wider podcast project as optimistic AI education through experimentation and terminology. Personal anecdotes and episode previews support that educational stance, but do not establish the legal, regulatory, employment or performance conclusions suggested by their titles.

qs.q: (That longevity is part of why we’re successful: we have experts who have been around for a long time doing excellent work.) But, like in any legacy successful organization, it’s really hard to pivot to do something that might disrupt what you’re doing today.

vlens.an: This curated legal-tech-vendor source accepts the cluster’s proposition that AI may expand dispute resolution beyond incremental assistance and materially develops its central distinction between assisted and machine adjudication. Arbitrus is presented as an autopilot model: end-to-end automation with an AI decision-maker replacing, rather than supporting, a human arbitrator. The founders justify that approach through predicted reductions in cost and resolution time, greater consistency and predictability, advance assessment of contractual claims, dispute prevention and, eventually, a private arbitration system handling disputes now reaching courts. There is material variation within the source: the founders advocate replacement strongly, whereas host Bob Ambrogi leaves open whether legal decision-making fundamentally requires human judgment. Moreover, the claimed benefits remain promises supported only by reported company testing without supplied methodology or independent validation; this limitation reinforces the cluster’s conclusion that efficiency and reliability claims exceed the available evidence. The source extends the machine-adjudication side of the proposition but does not directly substantiate the cluster’s access-to-justice case, focusing more on arbitration and general-counsel use.

qs.q: Instead, we're able to automate that entire system, end to end, from uploading the briefs, making the arguments, uploading evidence, and having an actual AI decision maker.
qs.a: Ep 280: Is Arbitrus.ai the Future of Dispute Resolution? · Legal-tech vendor · 2025

qs.q: The system promises to cut the cost of arbitration from an average of $100,000 to just $10,000 while delivering consistent, unbiased decisions within 72 hours.

vlens.an: The supplied source supports the cluster’s implementation-focused proposition, but only on organisational transformation rather than the central boundary between AI assistance and machine adjudication. McCormack anticipates AI disruption and argues that AAA’s accumulated expertise is simultaneously an enabling asset and a source of institutional inertia. Her practical response is deliberate change management, supplemented—but not replaced—by inorganic growth. This aligns with the synthesis’s view that adopting AI requires process and organisational redesign, while enthusiasm and strategy should not be mistaken for demonstrated performance. The source does not provide evidence on access gains, adjudicative reliability, or whether AI should assist or replace human arbitrators. Because this professional-voice category contains only one curated source here, no broader prevalence or meaningful cross-source variation can be inferred; the material variation within the source is chiefly between valuing legacy expertise and recognising that the same legacy impedes change.

qs.q: (That longevity is part of why we’re successful: we have experts who have been around for a long time doing excellent work.) But, like in any legacy successful organization, it’s really hard to pivot to do something that might disrupt what you’re doing today.

qs.q: You need a real plan for that, and change management is part of it.

vlens.an: The substantively relevant sources in this curated professional voice support the proposition that AI may expand dispute resolution through lower-cost, redesigned processes, while treating assistance and machine adjudication as materially different. The clearest institutional approaches are bounded and human-reviewed: AAA’s initial AI arbitrator drafts awards for a narrow case type while a human arbitrator verifies and approves the decision, and Pennsylvania’s interim judicial policy limits generative AI to approved, low-risk support tasks with human review, confidentiality protections and oversight. The shared reasons are access to justice, process suitability, domain expertise, party choice and procedural legitimacy. These sources also generally match the synthesis’s evidentiary caution: claimed reductions in cost and time, increased caseloads and improved confidence are expectations or implementation goals rather than demonstrated outcomes. Material variation concerns how far adjudicative automation might eventually go. McCormack preserves human-led options but leaves open removing the human if users request it; Abramowitz more directly challenges resistance to adjudicator AI by stressing human fallibility. Neither supplies comparative evidence that autonomous adjudication is equivalent or superior. Many other excerpts are introductions, personal-use anecdotes or discussions of education and professional adaptation; they are insufficiently substantive and should not be treated as additional support or opposition. One source redirects toward AI-enabled ADR education, but that different emphasis does not displace the voice’s overall support for the proposition.

elens.an: The 2023–2024 material supports the proposition’s early core: generative AI is presented chiefly as a means to redesign dispute-resolution processes, match lighter-touch procedures to particular disputes, and reach civil legal needs that conventional legal services cannot economically serve. The most substantive source treats human involvement as context-dependent—online dispute resolution may operate with or without a mediator—rather than endorsing autonomous adjudication across all matters. It also supplies a concrete assistive implementation, Clause Builder AI, built from AAA expertise and data. However, the claimed gains in access, speed, fairness and trust are aspirations or predictions, not measured outcomes, accuracy findings or comparative evidence. Internal variation is material: the Frances Kellor bot is only an exploratory, community-facing tool; several excerpts merely introduce AI literacy, courts, ethics or cross-professional comparisons and therefore do not establish a position; and the NotebookLM discussion redirects toward repackaging ADR education. Thus, this curated period supports process redesign and access expansion, while offering little evidence on the later cluster divide between human-verified awards and end-to-end machine adjudication, and little developed treatment of validation, legitimacy or governance safeguards.

qs.q: As Colin Rule, the CEO of ODR.com, says: “We want to fit the forum to the fuss.” And sometimes, an ODR product—an online dispute resolution product, maybe with a mediator and maybe without—could be a better forum for a particular fuss.

elens.an: The 2025 sources support the proposition that AI could expand and redesign dispute resolution, while preserving a crucial distinction between assistance and machine adjudication. Common supporting reasons include lowering procedural and cost barriers for valid but unmet civil claims, redesigning workflows around specific dispute types and user needs, and using human verification, confidentiality controls, staged deployment and party choice to protect legitimacy. They also consistently warrant evidentiary caution: projected gains in cost, speed, caseload, settlement and procedural confidence are largely expectations, company claims or internally reported tests rather than independently validated outcomes. Material internal variation concerns the appropriate degree of automation. AAA describes narrow, domain-specific systems in which AI drafts or supports decisions while a human arbitrator verifies the award; Fortuna Arbitration instead proposes end-to-end replacement of human arbitrators. Several other excerpts merely introduce adjacent topics or personal uses and are insufficient to determine a position. This assessment concerns only the curated sources supplied and does not indicate how prevalent these views were in 2025.

qs.q: This is an AI system that will actually draft arbitration awards with a human arbitrator validating and signing off on the final decision before it goes out.
qs.a: An AI Arbitrator? The Latest Innovations from the American Arbitration Association, with CEO Bridget McCormack and CTO Diana Didia · Regulators & courts · 2025

qs.q: Instead, we're able to automate that entire system, end to end, from uploading the briefs, making the arguments, uploading evidence, and having an actual AI decision maker.

elens.an: The 2026 material provides limited but directionally supportive evidence for the proposition. The only excerpt that substantively addresses adjudication supports reconsidering resistance to judicial and arbitral AI by comparing it with fallible human decision-making, while also acknowledging concrete courtroom hallucination cases and sanctions. It further preserves the proposition’s important distinction between AI decision support for judges and an AI arbitrator, rather than treating all adjudicative uses as equivalent. Material internal variation is primarily one of relevance and evidentiary depth: the remaining excerpts introduce in-house AI, creative lawyers, recording tools, unauthorized-practice allegations, AI governance, Legal Context Protocol, and private-equity interest, but do not develop positions on access to dispute resolution, human verification versus autonomous adjudication, legitimacy, safeguards, or comparative performance. Accordingly, they are unclear rather than contrary. Even the supportive adjudication source supplies framing and descriptions of emerging tools, not evidence that either assisted or autonomous adjudication improves access, reliability, cost, or outcomes.
